Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

vignette: Mrs. Lan is a 57-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who has been working as a midwife for over three decades. Married and deeply dedicated to her profession, she finds herself increasingly entangled in a web of anxiety stemming from a traumatic event—a rape that occurred six months ago. The day began like any other at the hospital where Mrs. Lan works. The air was thick with the scent of antiseptic and burnt coffee as she made her rounds, checking on new mothers and their newborns. However, it was an unusual patient who would change everything. As she entered a room to assist in delivering a baby, she found herself confronted by an intruder. The experience was jarring; the smell of his cologne mixed with the burnt coffee in the air, leaving her reeling. Since then, Mrs. Lan has been haunted by specific triggers that evoke memories of this traumatic event. She feels uncomfortable whenever she enters certain areas of the hospital, particularly those where the faint scent of burnt items lingers. The mere thought of being seen in these places heightens her sense of vulnerability. Her fear is not just of being physically harmed again but also of being judged or misunderstood by others. The intrusion monitoring has become a constant presence in her life. At home, she listens intently for any sounds that might indicate someone entering the house. This hyper-vigilance extends to her observations of people's faces and body language as well. She studies them meticulously, convinced that subtle cues will reveal potential threats. The physical reactivity is equally distressing; even minor triggers can lead to a surge of anxiety, rapid heartbeat, and sweating. Mrs. Lan’s fear of being seen in certain areas at the hospital has led her to avoid these places whenever possible. This avoidance not only limits her professional activities but also creates tension with her colleagues, who do not fully understand her reluctance. Her husband notices changes in her demeanor; she is more withdrawn and often preoccupied with thoughts about safety. The triggers have reinforced her sense of threat. Every time she encounters a situation that reminds her of the traumatic event—such as the smell of burnt items or feeling self-conscious in certain areas—the physical reactivity intensifies, deepening her fear. This cycle has become increasingly tight; the more she feels threatened, the more she avoids and monitors for triggers. Mrs. Lan’s avoidance behavior has led to a significant decline in her work performance. She is less able to focus on her duties as a midwife, which not only affects her own satisfaction but also impacts her ability to provide care to new mothers and their babies. The cumulative effect of these changes has strained her relationships with both colleagues and family members. What finally brought Mrs. Lan to seek help was the realization that she could no longer cope with the constant fear and avoidance. She is most afraid of being alone or vulnerable, yet she also hopes for a return to normalcy—a life where she can work without being constantly on edge and trust her environment again. The cumulative weight of these symptoms has made it clear to Mrs. Lan that professional help is necessary. She understands the need to address both the triggers and the sense of threat they evoke, hoping to regain control over her daily life and professional responsibilities.
